title: European Ash: Ancient Ash Trees You Can Visit
meta_description: Ash dieback is working west across Europe, which changes how you look at an old one. Lithuania's Witch's Ash is 7.41 metres round.
intro: Ash is the tree Europe is losing right now. A fungus from east Asia, harmless to the ashes it evolved alongside, was first noticed in Poland in the early 1990s and has since worked its way west across the continent, which puts a different weight on every old one still standing. Lithuania's thickest, the Witch's Ash at Plateliai, is 7.41 metres round and looks like four trees knotted together, which local legend says it once was. In Stockholm, Carl Linnaeus wrote down Valkasken, the burl ash, in the 1740s, and it is still there on Langholmen. Gdansk's Ash of King Jan is 6.1 metres round. Prague's grows to 37 metres in the one corner of Strahov Monastery the monks left open to the public. And in Giethoorn an ash has heaved the ground under a farmhouse into a mound.
